newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: WI discussing Global Wool with Australian watchdog.
newsitem.headline: WI discussing Global Wool with Australian watchdog.

text.p: Discussions were progressing with the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) over the proposed formation of Global Wool, Wool International (WI) chairman Dick Warburton said on Thursday.

WI, which is in charge of selling Australia's 1.7 million bale wool stockpile, has proposed forming a three-way wool merchanting and risk management group, Global Wool, with pastoral houses Elders Ltd and Wesfarmers Dalgety Ltd.
"Further discussions are taking place between the ACCC and the three venture partners to clarify the situation," he told the Wool Council of Australia annual conference.

"While delays to the venture can be frustrating, one aspect of the project that has been gratifying to WI is that the project has raised the level of awareness among woolgrowers and woolbrokers of the need for risk management and forward marketing," Warburton said.
The intention remained that equal access to wool through Global Wool would be allowed for all brokers and exporters, he said.
The proposed joint-venture with Elders and Wesfarmers Dalgety was was on practical considerations of forming a venture with good critical mass, he said.
The anti-monopoly watchdog recently raised objections on competition grounds.
Global Wool has been seen as incorporating an investment trust in which woolgrowers might invest proceeds from their equity in WI, held through their stake in the wool stockpile.
This has been seen as leading to a possible float of Global Wool to the Australian share market.

WI's role would continue only until the last stockpile bale of wool had been sold and net proceeds distributed to those woolgrowers and parties who held equity entitlements, Warburton said on Thursday.
Answering questions from the floor, Warburton said WI had received several approaches for the purchase of Australia's entire wool stockpile.
All offers would be examined, but legislation required WI to act flexibly and equitably for all woolgrowers, he said.
WI was still waiting to receive formal proposals but if any appeared attractive, a sale of the entire stockpile would probably have to go to a full tender process, he said.
